bib.title: GPT-NeoX-20B: An Open-Source Autoregressive Language Model
bib.venue: Proceedings of BigScience Episode #5 Workshop on Challenges & Perspectives in Creating Large Language Models

read.skipped: References skimmed; tokenization example figures (12-17) and Hendrycks per-subject tables 10-13 not examined cell by cell.

question: Can a 20B-parameter dense autoregressive LLM be trained on the Pile and released openly, and how does it compare with GPT-3, FairSeq and GPT-J on language, math and knowledge tasks?
contributions: Release of GPT-NeoX-20B weights (plus checkpoints every 1000 steps) under a permissive license
Release of training and evaluation code (gpt-neox)
Architecture/tokenizer changes vs GPT-3: rotary embeddings, parallel attention+FF, new Pile-trained BPE tokenizer, all dense layers
Evaluation against GPT-3 (API), FairSeq and GPT-J-6B

method.summary: Decoder-only transformer, 44 layers, hidden 6144, 64 heads, trained on the Pile for 150,000 steps at batch ~3.15M tokens with AdamW, with hyperparameters interpolated from GPT-3. Uses rotary embeddings on 25% of dims, parallel attention/FF, and a new 50257-token BPE tokenizer trained on the Pile. Evaluated zero- and five-shot with the EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness.
method.task: next-token pretraining; evaluation on NLU, arithmetic/MATH and Hendrycks multi-subject QA

datasets.name: The Pile
datasets.preprocessing: Used as-is, no deduplication; some components up-sampled (inherent to the Pile)

datasets.name: NLU suite (ANLI, ARC, HeadQA, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, LogiQA, OpenBookQA, PiQA, PROST, QA4MRE, SciQ, TriviaQA, Winogrande, WSC)
MATH test and Brown et al. arithmetic

models.name: GPT-NeoX-20B
models.architecture: decoder-only transformer, GPT-3-like, all dense layers, parallel attention+FF, rotary
models.init_from: inferred: random init; Wang (2021) init for FF outputs, small init (Nguyen and Salazar 2019) elsewhere
models.tokenizer: BPE trained on the Pile, GPT-2-like

other.untied_layer_norms: two independent LayerNorms by oversight: x+Attn(LN1(x))+FF(LN2(x))

other.note: five-shot omitted for GPT-3 due to financial limitations

training.optimizer: AdamW, betas 0.9/0.95, eps 1.0E-8, with ZeRO stage 1
training.lr_schedule: cosine decay to 10% of original value at end of training
training.warmup: 0.01 (config; unit not stated, inferred: fraction of training)
training.batch_size: approximately 3.15M tokens, or 1538 contexts of 2048 tokens each
training.epochs: inferred: ~1.0+ epochs; paper notes training crossed the 1 epoch boundary (Fig 2)
training.hardware: twelve Supermicro AS-4124GO-NART servers, each 8x NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB (96 GPUs), 2x AMD EPYC 7532, InfiniBand; tensor parallel 2, pipeline parallel 4
training.compute: 117 teraFLOPS per GPU; 43.92 MWh electricity over 1830 hours of training; 66.24 MWh total incl. 920 further hours

other.hyperparameter tuning: none at full scale; weight decay from smaller-scale experiments; lr interpolated between GPT-3 13B and 175B
other.CO2: 31.73 metric tons for training; just under 35 with eval

inference.samples: zero-shot and five-shot; no seeds reported
inference.prompting: EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness task prompts (version 0); few-shot k=5 for five-shot

metrics.name: task accuracy
metrics.definition: Harness accuracy per task (reported as fraction; error is standard error)

metrics.name: tokens needed to encode corpus
metrics.definition: count of tokens from tokenizing a validation set

eval.protocol: Plots carry error bars of two standard errors (95% CI); no scaling-law curves fitted; human and random baselines where available

evidence.quote: we interpolate between the learning rates of their 13B and 175B models to arrive at a learning rate of 0.97E−5

results.claim: GPT-NeoX-20B tokenizer represents the Pile validation set with about 10% fewer tokens than GPT-2's
results.setup: Pile validation set, GPT-2 vs GPT-NeoX-20B tokenizers
results.quote:
Overall, the GPT-NeoX-20B tokenizer represents the Pile
validation set with approximately 10% fewer tokens compared to the GPT-2 tokenizer.

results.claim: Excluding whitespace tokens, NeoX tokenizer still uses 5% fewer tokens on the Pile validation set
results.setup: Pile validation set, whitespace tokens excluded
results.quote: We observe that the GPT-NeoX-20B tokenizer still uses 5% fewer tokens to represent the Pile validation set compared to the GPT-2 tokenizer.

results.claim: On C4 (out of domain) the two tokenizers use about the same number of tokens
results.quote:
We find that the GPT-NeoX-20B tokenizer tokenizes
the C4 validation set to approximately the same number of tokens as the GPT-2 tokenizer.

results.claim: Fig 1 code example: 55 tokens with GPT-2, 39 with GPT-NeoX-20B tokenizer
results.note: Quote omitted; value checked against figure text '39 tokens'.

results.claim: GitHub component needs 23% fewer tokens (ratio 0.76820) and PubMed Central 0.76545
results.quote:
with the biggest gains in whitespace heavy datasets such as arXiv, GitHub and
StackExchange

results.claim: Across 32 evaluations GPT-NeoX-20B beats FairSeq 13B on 22, loses on 4, ties on 6
results.setup: NLU tasks zero- and five-shot, vs FairSeq 13B
results.quote:
In total, across the 32 evaluations we did
we outpreform on 22 tasks, underpreform on four
tasks, and fall within the margin of error on six
tasks.

results.table: Table 2, row LAMBADA, column GPT-NeoX 20B (GPT-J 0.683±0.006; DaVinci 0.752±0.006)
Table 2 row HellaSwag col GPT-NeoX; Table 3 FairSeq 13B 0.554±0.005

results.claim: HellaSwag is the weakest result, four standard deviations below FairSeq 13B
results.quote:
By far our weakest performance is on Hel-
laSwag, where we score four standard deviations
below FairSeq 13B in both zero- and five-shot eval-
uations.

results.claim: Five-shot 5-digit-free arithmetic: 2-digit addition 0.992 for NeoX vs 0.880 for GPT-J
Five-shot MATH is near zero for all models, e.g. Algebra 0.049 NeoX
Going from 0 to 5 shots improves GPT-NeoX-20B by 0.0598 and FairSeq 13B by 0.0183
results.setup: average over tasks (aggregate not defined precisely)
results.quote:
When going from 0-shot to 5-shot evaluations, GPT-J-6B
improves by 0.0526 and GPT-NeoX-20B improves
by 0.0598 while the FairSeq 6.7B and 13B models
improve by 0.0051 and 0.0183 respectively.

results.claim: No validation-loss drop at epoch boundary: no gain seen from deduplication-free data crossing 1 epoch
results.quote:
even at the 20B parameter scale
we see no drop in test validation loss after crossing
the 1 epoch boundary.

results.claim: Training emitted 31.73 metric tons CO2, about 10% of Strubell et al.'s 284.01 t estimate
results.quote:
We found that the process of develop-
ing and training GPT-NeoX-20B emitted almost
exactly 10% of Strubell et al. (2019)’s estimate,
coming in at a total of 69957 lbs or 31.73 met-
ric tons of CO2.

results.claim: Training reached 117 TFLOPS per GPU with tensor parallel 2 and pipeline parallel 4
results.quote:
we were able to achieve and maintain an efficiency of 117
teraFLOPS per GPU.

results.claim: Parallel attention+FF gave 15% throughput increase in Mesh Transformer JAX with comparable early loss
results.quote:
In Mesh Transformer
JAX (Wang, 2021), this led to a 15% throughput
increase, while having comparable loss curves with
running them in series during early training.

limits: Hyperparameters were interpolated from GPT-3, not tuned; authors say they are 'almost certainly ... no longer optimal'
No coding evaluations, though design choices targeted code
No deduplication of the Pile; effect on downstream performance untested
Unintended untied layer norms; only small-scale experiments suggest no effect
GPT-3 five-shot not run; HellaSwag deficit 'largely inexplicable'
Pile vs GPT-3 data difference is the biggest unknown factor in comparisons
Tokenizer analysis uses Pile validation, in-domain for the tokenizer
Single training run, no seeds reported

lineage.quote: architecture largely follows that of GPT-3

lineage.note: authors saw no benefit from avoiding dedup at 20B but concede it is hard to dismiss
